clue.text: Agree, initially, about new hotel by new motorway

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: first letter of Agree

indicators.note: the first 'new' says the preceding word is made over into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
H is hotel in the phonetic alphabet
the second 'new' is the abbreviation N

explanation.surface: Someone nods agreement to a trip past a new hotel along a recently built motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' appears twice doing two jobs: first as the signal to rearrange ABOUT, then as plain N.
explanation.definitionFit: An autobahn is the German name for a high-speed highway, the equivalent of a British motorway.

clue.text: When one chooses a serge

parts.note: taken as written
serge is a kind of twill, a fabric with a diagonal weave

explanation.surface: A tailor's customer is choosing a serge cloth for a suit.
explanation.walkthrough: Serge looks like something chosen, but it stands for a specific fabric as an example of its type.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something at will means doing it whenever one pleases, an adverbial phrase matching the clause.

clue.text: Eat out, then secure the wherewithal for a drink

indicators.note: out suggests the word is put out of its usual order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
to bag something is to secure or capture it

explanation.surface: Someone dines out, then makes sure they have the means to pay for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wherewithal' suggests money for a round, but here it is the literal makings of a cuppa.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea bag holds the leaves needed to brew a cup of tea, the material for a hot beverage.

clue.text: Showman from Niagara River port shown on leaflet

parts.note: Buffalo, New York, stands at the head of the Niagara River on Lake Erie
a bill is a printed notice or handbill

explanation.surface: A showman from a lakeside American city is advertised on a flyer.
explanation.walkthrough: Buffalo Bill was William Cody, who toured his Wild West show across America and Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Buffalo Bill Cody ran a famous travelling Wild West spectacle, making him the classic frontier entertainer.

clue.text: One clasping crocodile in confusion?

parts.note: one who clasps someone is a hugger
the mugger is an Indian freshwater crocodile

explanation.surface: Someone tangled up with a crocodile, hugging it in the chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: The mugger crocodile is less familiar than the street robber the word usually means.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugger-mugger means muddle or disorder, and also secrecy; the jumbled sense matches confusion.

clue.text: Pale china stopper

parts.note: rhyming slang: china plate means mate, a friend
a lid is a cover that stops something up

explanation.surface: A description of a pale porcelain stopper for a bottle or jar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pale china' reads as a colour of porcelain; china is Cockney rhyming slang for a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Pallid is a synonym for pale, describing a face or complexion lacking colour.

clue.text: Commander from Niagara

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the next word as they stand

parts.note: the run of letters sits in the middle of Niagara

explanation.surface: An officer who has come from the Niagara region.
explanation.definitionFit: An aga was a military commander or chief officer in the Ottoman Empire, a title also used in crosswords.

clue.text: Star embraced by young woman in gambling centre

indicators.note: something embraced is held in the arms, so one piece is wrapped by the other

parts.note: a lass is a girl or young woman
Vega is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra

explanation.surface: A film star is hugged by a young woman at a casino.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' suggests a celebrity, but it is a real star in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Las Vegas in Nevada is famous for its casinos, the best-known gaming city in the world.

clue.text: Set off from public school in time

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other

parts.note: a date is a point in time
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Someone departs from their boarding school right on schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a public school is a fee-paying private school; Eton is the best known.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off an explosive is to detonate it, a transitive verb meaning to trigger a blast.

clue.text: Carry on about heading for Harwich, far off accommodation for ships

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece encloses the others

parts.note: to wage war is to carry it on

indicators.note: off implies the word has gone wrong and its letters are jumbled
the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Harwich
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Directions to keep going toward Harwich, a port, far off where ships berth.
explanation.walkthrough: Harwich is a port on the Essex coast, which makes the shipping surface convincing.
explanation.definitionFit: Wharfage is room at a wharf for vessels to moor, or the fee charged for using it.

clue.text: Dog's strong point after bit of breeding

indicators.note: a bit of a word is one letter, here its first

parts.note: first letter of breeding
an asset is a strength or advantage

explanation.surface: A dog's best quality comes from a bit of good breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog's' reads as possessive, but the 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A basset is a short-legged hound breed with long ears, used for tracking scent.

clue.text: Travelling OK, on reliable part of the London Underground

indicators.note: travelling things move about, so the letters change places

parts.note: the letters of these three words, taken together

explanation.surface: A commuter reports that the Tube is running fine and is dependable.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the indicator and the definition in one picture of a Tube journey.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bakerloo line is one of the London Underground's routes, named from Baker Street and Waterloo.

clue.text: Monk astride large beast of burden

indicators.note: a rider astride sits with legs either side, so one piece straddles another

parts.note: a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A monk riding a big pack animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The L slots in after the first letter of LAMA, giving a double L.
explanation.definitionFit: The llama is a South American animal domesticated to carry loads, a classic pack animal.

clue.text: Disabled, one during dash in battle

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so these letters go inside

parts.note: elan is flair or dash
lame means disabled in the leg
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An injured soldier makes a run for it during combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' looks like a verb of flight in a war story, but it is the noun for verve, which wraps the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: El Alamein in Egypt was the site of decisive Second World War engagements in 1942.

clue.text: Accomplices in case? Scores, I suspect

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

parts.note: the letters of these three words, taken together

explanation.surface: A detective muses that dozens of people helped in a criminal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' and 'Accomplices' build a police picture; suspect is the anagram signal, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In law an accessory is someone who helps a criminal before or after the crime, a partner in guilt.

clue.text: Pessimist's frame of mind in retreat, confronting trader

indicators.note: a retreating army goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: mood is a frame of mind
a merchant is a trader

explanation.surface: A gloomy person's withdrawn state of mind as they face a shopkeeper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pessimist's' looks possessive; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A doom merchant is someone who constantly predicts disaster, an idiom for a gloomy prophet.

clue.text: Mean to travel round with one learner driver in the gloaming

indicators.note: travelling round something means encircling it, so one piece wraps the rest

parts.note: tight means stingy
W is a standard abbreviation for with
I is the Roman numeral one
an L-plate marks a learner driver

explanation.surface: A miserly instructor drives around at dusk with a novice at the wheel.
explanation.walkthrough: Gloaming is a Scottish word for dusk; W, I and L go inside TIGHT after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The gloaming is the half-light after sunset, the same as dusk or evening dimness.

clue.text: Lacking practical expertise, member beginning to criticise musical

parts.note: an arm is a limb, a member of the body

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of criticise
Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A theatre critic with no real stage experience pans a musical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club member, but it is a limb; Hair is the famous 1967 hippie musical.
explanation.definitionFit: An armchair critic or general theorises from comfort without hands-on experience; the adjective means theoretical.

clue.text: Labour group on seminar

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
a seminar is a small teaching class

explanation.surface: A Labour Party study group attending a seminar.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is the UK's left-wing party, traditionally associated with this group; 'Labour' looks like the party but means manual workers.
explanation.definitionFit: The working class is the social group of people doing manual or wage labour.

clue.text: Sculpted figure, say, university acquired

indicators.note: what is acquired is taken in, so one piece holds the other

parts.note: to state is to say
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A university bought a carved figure, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like 'for example' but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A statue is a carved or cast representation of a person or animal.

clue.text: Jacket in tan, or a khaki

indicators.note: in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A shopper choosing a coat in one of two earthy colours.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is a waterproof hooded coat, a kind of outdoor jacket.

clue.text: Picture that woman getting in pub round

indicators.note: getting in means entering, so one piece goes inside the others

parts.note: your local is your neighbourhood pub
O is round in shape
her is the pronoun for that woman

explanation.surface: A photo of a woman buying a round of drinks at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Picture means film here; Local Hero is Bill Forsyth's 1983 Scottish comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Local Hero is a well-known British film, and picture is an old word for a movie.

clue.text: Playwright from Troon? Unlikely

indicators.note: unlikely suggests an improbable version, so the letters come out rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Doubting that a dramatist comes from a Scottish golfing town.
explanation.walkthrough: Troon is a town on the Ayrshire coast in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Orton was an English dramatist of the 1960s, author of Loot and Entertaining Mr Sloane.

clue.text: Batsman's stroke, good cut

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to lance a boil is to cut it open

explanation.surface: A cricketer plays a fine shot, a well-timed cut.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a cut is itself a stroke, so 'good cut' reads as more cricket, but cut means to lance.
explanation.definitionFit: A glance is a cricket shot deflecting the ball off the bat's face behind the wicket.

clue.text: Hint, hint left ignored

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: a clue is a hint
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone drops a hint, and the hint goes unheeded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' reads as 'remaining', but it is the letter L removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cue is a signal or prompt, the same as a hint about what to do.

clue.text: Clergyman, one entering cathedral

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so this letter goes into the other word

parts.note: a minster is a large church, like York Minster
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A priest walks into a cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister is a member of the clergy, especially in Protestant churches.

clue.text: Sailor needs to be given purpose

parts.note: a tar is an old word for a sailor
to get something is to be given it

explanation.surface: A seaman needs a sense of direction in life.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is an aim or goal, so it serves as a synonym for an intended objective.

clue.text: Information on summit in bureaucratic language

parts.note: news is information
a peak is a summit

explanation.surface: Officialese used to report on a mountain summit, or a summit meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Newspeak is Orwell's invented language from Nineteen Eighty-Four.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspeak now means deliberately ambiguous official jargon, after Orwell's state-controlled tongue.
